## NL to query spec

All systems run locally under vLLM on one H200 (GPU 4), with guided JSON decoding and thinking off. "Exec acc" means
executing the predicted spec returns the same rows as the expected spec (ties order-insensitive, `query/compare.py`).
Raw numbers are in `results.json`, and the questions each system got wrong are in `runs/eval_<system>_<dataset>.json`.

| System | Valid JSON % | Exec acc % (generated test) | Exec acc % (dev/hard) | Exec acc % (independent) | Exec acc % (hand-written) | Hallucinated-number rate | Latency p50 / p95 (s) | Weights in GPU memory (GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-32B few-shot (teacher) | 100.0 | 99.8 (n=443) | 94.4 (n=18) | 80.5 (n=297) | pending | not measured | 1.473 / 1.571 | 61.03 |
| Base Qwen3-8B few-shot | 100.0 | 96.8 (n=443) | 94.4 (n=18) | 75.1 (n=297) | pending | not measured | 0.439 / 0.469 | 15.27 |

Validation split (n=386): teacher 98.7, base 8B 93.0, SFT 98.2. Throughput at
48 concurrent requests on the generated test split: teacher 21.7 q/s, base 8B 40.8
q/s, SFT 43.1 q/s. Latency is single sequential requests.

### How to read this

- **The generated test split flatters the teacher.** A paraphrase was kept only if the teacher translated it back
  to the original spec, so on paraphrases the teacher is right by construction. Only template questions can catch
  it out. The SFT student matching it there (99.8 vs 99.8) is the meaningful part.
- **Dev/hard is small (n=18), and it is not untouched.** The pilot's dev/hard misses (a limit of one on plural
  questions with no number) led to a template fix before the full run. Treat it as a dev set. The independent set
  (below) and the hand-written set are the real tests.
- **The base 8B is a strong baseline.** Its spec accuracy is lower than its execution accuracy (test
  94.8 vs 96.8, dev/hard 83.3 vs 94.4): many of its specs
  differ from the expected one but return the same rows.

### What fine-tuning fixed

The teacher's systematic error is reading a position family as a single group. 26 of its
36 misses on correct-by-construction template questions were this ("Which midfielder ..." to `[CM]`,
"Which forward ..." to `[ST]`). The same error drops Brozović from "Which Croatian midfielders completed the most
passes under pressure?". The SFT student, trained on templates that use the documented convention, gets these right,
including the Brozović question.

### Known issues

- **Teacher bias leaks into a few labels.** 4 of 3,925 pairs (3 train,
  0 val, 1 test) have a paraphrase that turned "striker" into "forward" while keeping the
  label `[ST]`, because the teacher's round-trip accepted it. 1 of the student's
  1 test misses is one of these: it answered `[ST, W]`, which is the documented convention. Left as
  measured, not relabelled after the fact.
- **Name copying.** The student sometimes "corrects" a misspelled or accented name instead of copying it
  ("Theo Hernédez", "Firas Albirkan"). Resolution then fails, and the pipeline answers "Did you mean ...?" instead of
  guessing.
- **Resolver fix after the frozen independent runs.** The surname step used to match any name token, so "Woo-Young
  Jun" (a misspelling of Jung Woo-Young) resolved silently to Son Jun-Ho, and "Luis Sosa" to Borna Sosa. It now needs
  the player's last name token, and a lone surname match is rejected if the other words do not share an initial with
  his names; initials never choose between players. "Woo-Young Jun" now gets "Did you mean Jung Woo-Young?", and
  "Neymar Jr" is an alias of Neymar (`tests/test_executor.py`). No gold spec in any set resolves differently. The
  frozen numbers were scored with the old resolver and are not re-run; the Woo-Young question fails either way.
  The fix also exposed two training targets that say "Kevin Noppert": the paraphraser invented the first name and the
  old guess (Andries Noppert) let it through the round trip. They now get "Did you mean", which re-keys one spec in
  the list of specs already in use. The independent set is still disjoint from all of them.
- **Ambiguous paraphrases** account for most of the rest (passes "managed" under pressure: attempted or completed?).

## Independent test set (non-Qwen question writer)

Built to remove the teacher bias of the generated split: the questions come from a different model family, and no
round-trip filter decides which ones survive. Files: `independent_test.jsonl` (297 questions),
`independent_misspelled.jsonl` (20), `independent_dropped.jsonl` (3).

**How it was built**

- **Specs, sampled in code** (`independent_specs.py`, seed 2026). The sampler is the one behind the training
  data, drawn from cycling decks so that every metric (19 of 19), every position group and
  family, every stage (the third-place match alone, which the training sampler never draws, included), every team as
  an opponent and every team as a team filter appear. 60 questions rank teams and 72 name
  players. A spec is excluded if it equals any of the 2029 specs already in use (re-checked by `eval.report`): every spec sampled for
  the training data (`data/specs.jsonl`, including specs whose questions were all dropped), train, val, test,
  dev/hard and the few-shot examples. Specs with an empty result, and player specs where a named player did not play
  in the filtered matches, are dropped at sampling, before any model sees them.
- **Questions, written by `mistralai/Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501`** (`independent_questions.py`, served by
  `scripts/serve_generator.sh`). The writer gets a plain-English brief of each spec (the statistic in everyday
  words, the ranking, each filter) and never sees the schema, field names, position codes, the translation prompt or
  any model's output. One casual fan question per spec, at temperature 0.8. 88 of the
  300 briefs, chosen in code before generation, ask for typos and slang. Player names are to be written
  exactly as given, because a misspelled name correctly ends in "Did you mean ...?" and could never count as right;
  misspellings are tested in their own subset. There is **no teacher round-trip filter**.
- **One prompt revision, before any system was run.** In the first generation the single-player brief read like a
  ranking prompt, so several lookups came back as rankings with no player named. The single-player and comparison
  briefs were made explicit and the whole set was generated again once. That second generation is final. The first
  is kept in `logs/` (local only).
- **Name check, before any system was run** (`independent_name_check.py`, deterministic). Every player and team the
  question names is compared with the gold spec. Clear mismatches were dropped:
  - "How does Cody Gakpo's and Darwin  Nunez's xT  by passing and carrying the ball compare in the knockout rounds, mate?": writer error: the spec compares Cody Gakpo and Achraf Dari (written "Dari"); the question names Darwin Núñez instead of Dari.
  - "Who do you think pressed more? How many times did Christian Pulisic, Aaron Mooy and Goncalo Guedes press  opponents on the ball during the 2022 World Cup in Qatar?": writer error: the spec is about Diogo Costa, Riley McGree and Rodrigo De Paul (written "Costa", "McGree", "Paul"); the question names Christian Pulisic, Aaron Mooy and Gonçalo Guedes.
  - "How many progressive passes 90 per game did Ederson Varela make in the 2022 World Cup Qatar?": writer error: the spec is about Guillermo Varela (written "Varela"); the question calls him "Ederson Varela", borrowing the first name of another player (Ederson, Brazil).
  Kept despite a flag: a ranking question that ends with a guess at the answer ("someone like Messi or Neymar"),
  since the ask itself is clear, and 5 questions whose player or team names only match fuzzily because
  the writer misspelled them anyway ("urugay", "Rapinah", "Rabman"). For a misspelled player name, a system that
  copies it gets "Did you mean ...?", which counts as wrong here. The other questions are kept exactly as written, including loose phrasings.

**Misspelled-name subset.** 20 single-player questions (7 dropped letter, 7 swapped letters, 6 missing accent), on specs disjoint from everything
above. The writer gets the correct name and the code then swaps in the planned misspelling, so each question carries
exactly one controlled error. A question passes if the system's spec returns the right rows (it fixed the name), or
stops at "Did you mean ...?" with the right player as the first suggestion. It is scored on its own and never mixed
into the main accuracy. **The ceiling for copying the name verbatim is 19 of 20:**
for "Thaigo Silva" (Thiago Silva) the first suggestion is Bernardo Silva. So a system that copies names exactly cannot pass every question; one that corrects the name
itself still can.

### Results on the independent set

Each system was run once on the final set (`eval.run_eval`, one GPU job at a time), and nothing was changed after
seeing the results.

| | Qwen3-32B teacher | Base Qwen3-8B | SFT Qwen3-8B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valid JSON % (n=297) | 100.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| **Exec acc %** (n=297) | **80.5** | **75.1** | **80.8** |
| Exec acc % on the checker-validated subset (post hoc, n=117) | 94.0 | 85.5 | 95.7 |
| Spec acc % (n=297) | 77.4 | 68.4 | 78.5 |
| Latency p50 (s) | 1.534 | 0.455 | 0.448 |
| **Misspelled-name pass %** (n=20, separate subset) | **90.0** (11 fixed the name, 7 "Did you mean" with the right player) | **90.0** (6 fixed the name, 12 "Did you mean" with the right player) | **90.0** (6 fixed the name, 12 "Did you mean" with the right player) |

- **The teacher's edge from the round-trip filter is gone.** SFT 80.8, teacher 80.5, base 8B
  75.1. On the generated test split the same systems score 99.8, 99.8 and
  96.8: the filter kept only questions the teacher already reads correctly, and these questions were not
  filtered at all.
- **Much of the gap to a perfect score is label noise.** 41 questions are missed by all three systems,
  usually with the same spec from each (`runs/independent_all_failed.json`). Read by hand, nearly all are writer
  errors that a round trip would have caught: the writer dropped the requested count ("Who scored the most goals
  for South Korea?" for a top five), turned a team ranking into a player ranking, named a different statistic
  (completed instead of attempted passes), or wrote "per game" for a total. They are left as labelled, so absolute
  accuracy here is a lower bound, and the set is best read as a comparison between systems on the same noisy questions.
- **Label validation (post hoc, secondary).** After the frozen runs, `mistralai/Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501` checked every question
  against the plain-English reading of its gold spec (the interpretation echo, never the JSON) and answered whether
  the question asks for exactly that (`label_validation.py`; verdicts and the exact prompt in `label_validation.json`).
  It never saw any system's output, and the rule and prompt were committed before it checked any question. It
  accepted 117 of 297. On that subset: SFT 95.7, teacher 94.0, base 8B 85.5
  (the post hoc row in the table). The frozen full-set numbers stay the main result. Two cautions:
  - **The checker is the same model that wrote the questions**, so it can share the writer's misreadings and pass a
    question it wrote badly. It is not an independent judge.
  - **It is strict and noisy.** It rejected 3 of the 3 questions dropped before the
    runs and 38 of the 41 questions every system missed, but read by hand many of its
    rejections are spurious: it rejects "the top N players" against a reading of "the N players", and calls "pass
    accuracy" and "pass completion %" different statistics. So the subset is smaller than the set of good labels, and
    it leans towards plainly worded questions.
- **Misspelled names:** teacher 90.0, base 8B 90.0, SFT 90.0. All three miss the same
  two questions. One is "Thaigo Silva" (the ceiling above). The other is a writer error: for the spec's "McGree"
  (Riley McGree) the writer wrote "Aaron McGree", so the misspelled question names nobody who exists and gets no
  suggestion. The teacher more often fixes the name itself; the 8B models copy it and let "Did you mean" catch it.

## Hallucinated numbers: naive LLM vs the pipeline

Run with `python -m eval.hallucination` (GPU). Results are in `hallucination.json`, per-question answers and scores
in `runs/hallucination_records.json`. `--rescore` re-scores the saved answers with the current verifier.

- **Naive:** Qwen3-32B with the whole player table in its context (players with 90+ minutes,
  32k tokens of prompt) and the pipeline's conventions in its prompt, answering directly at
  temperature 0.7.
- **Pipeline:** SFT 8B spec, then executed result, then Qwen3-32B answer from the rows, then the verifier.
- **Scoring:** both are checked against the **ground-truth** result (the expected spec, executed) with the same frozen
  verifier (`query/verify.py`). A player's other true tournament stats also count as true, so citing them is not
  penalised.
- **Questions:** the generated test split plus dev/hard, 461 in all (never the hand-written set). The
  comparison uses the 290 player questions the naive model can fairly answer: no stage or opponent filter, and
  every ground-truth player is in its table. Team questions are excluded because the table omits players under
  90 minutes.

### Results on the same 290 questions

| System | Answers scored | Hallucinated number | Wrong player or team | Order error | Any verified error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Naive: Qwen3-32B + full stats table in context | 290 of 290 | 33.1% (96) | 69.3% (201) | 8.3% (24) | **78.6% (228)** |
| Pipeline: SFT 8B spec + executor + Qwen3-32B answer (raw, before correction) | 289 of 290 | 0.0% (0) | 0.3% (1) | 0.0% (0) | **0.3% (1)** |

Rates are % of answers scored, with the count in brackets. Columns:

- **Answers scored:** questions that got an answer. The naive model answers everything; the pipeline replied "Did you mean ...?" to 1 misspelled name instead of answering.
- **Hallucinated number:** at least one number that is neither in the ground-truth result nor any true tournament stat of the player it is attached to (verifier issue kinds `number` and `attribution`).
- **Wrong player or team:** names at least one player or team that is not in the ground-truth result or the question's filters (kinds `name` and `team`).
- **Order error:** lists result players out of rank order, or gives one a wrong ordinal (kind `order`).
- **Any verified error:** at least one of the three. The columns overlap, so they do not add up.

### Why 33.1% and 78.6% are both right

They count different things over the same 290 naive answers, and one contains the other:

- **96 answers (33.1%)** contain at least one false number.
- **228 answers (78.6%)** contain at least one verified error of any kind. That includes the
  96 above.
- **The other 132 answers (45.5%)** have no false number the verifier can pin down, but name a
  player or team that is not in the ground-truth result (132 of the 132). Typically the
  model lists the wrong players, often with their true numbers: asked for the five players with the most progressive
  carries, it lists Ziyech, Lautaro Martínez and Morata, with their real totals, among the top five
  (`examples.md`, example 5).

A number attached to a player outside the result cannot be compared with a row, so it is only checked against the
pool of true numbers for every player the answer names. Many numbers in wrong-player answers therefore pass, which is
one reason the 33.1% is a lower bound on false numbers.

**The pipeline's single error** (1 of 289) is a spec disagreement, not a hallucination:
asked "Which forward had the highest goal total in the 2022 World Cup?", it answered "Kylian Mbappé had the highest goal total in the 2022 World Cup with 8 goals." (Kylian Mbappé is not in the verified result). This is the one test question whose label was contaminated by the "forward" bias (Known issues
above). The answer is right under the documented convention.

**Correction to the earlier table.** The pipeline's "any verified error" was previously reported as
0.0%. That figure checked pipeline answers against the pipeline's *own* executed result, while the
naive column used ground truth.
Against ground truth it is 0.3%, as in the table above.

### How much to trust the naive numbers

- **Precision (hand audit):** Of 15† randomly sampled flagged naive numbers (my audit during development), 13† are clear hallucinations, 1† was truncation ("271 minutes" for 271.7; now accepted), and 1† is unclear (correct arithmetic, "135/153 = 88.23%", for an unidentified player). A blind audit of 40 answers (20 flagged, 20 passed, verdicts hidden) is in `audit_sample.md`, waiting to be marked.
- **A lower bound in another sense:** a number only counts as hallucinated if it is not *any* true stat of the
  player it is attached to, so a wrong number that equals another of his true stats slips through. For example,
  tournament totals presented as per-90 values pass (`examples.md`, example 8).
- **Unknown names:** names outside the dataset (for example "Péter Gulácsi (Hungary)", who was not at the tournament)
  are invisible to the name check. Their invented numbers are still flagged.
- **Negative numbers:** the verifier reads numbers without their sign. No ground-truth value in these question sets
  is negative, so it changed no score here, but a correct negative xT value would be flagged.
- **Sensitivity:** naive answers are sampled at temperature 0.7, and the rate moved between
  development runs as the verifier was fixed (see the audit trail below). Read it as "roughly a third of naive
  answers contain a false number", not as a precise figure.

Real catches, with the true values and what the verifier did, are in `examples.md`. Every catch from the final runs
is in `logs/verifier_catches.jsonl` (local only).

## Verifier error-injection test

Run with `python -m eval.verifier_injection --seed N`. Results are in `verifier_injection*.json`.

- **Base answers:** the pipeline's 459 answers that are correct and verify clean against ground truth.
- **Method:** one programmatic error of each applicable type is injected into each answer, and the runtime verifier
  (no extra truth) is run on the result.
- **Logging:** every catch is logged with `source: error_injection`.

Seeds 0 and 1 were used while fixing the verifier, so the held-out figures below are **seed 2**, run
once on the final answers with the verifier frozen.

| Injected error | n | Caught % | Right issue kind % | Restored exactly by auto-correction % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| number_perturb | 400 | 100.0 | 100.0 | 97.8 |
| value_swap | 236 | 100.0 | 100.0 | 97.5 |
| name_swap | 400 | 100.0 | 100.0 | n/a |
| team_swap | 373 | 100.0 | 100.0 | n/a |
| order_swap | 227 | 100.0 | 100.0 | n/a |
| fabricated_stat | 400 | 99.5 | 99.5 | n/a |
| **Overall** | 2036 | **99.9** | 99.9 | |

- **False positives:** 0 of the 459 clean answers were flagged. Seed 0 gives 100.0% caught
  and 0 false positives.
- **The 2 held-out misses:** in 2 of them, the injected number also appears in
  the question ("Jong also recorded 22 pressures." added to the answer for "who r the 10 def midz wiht most xg in wc 22, plz 450 min cutof"). Numbers quoted from the question are allowed by design.
- **When the correction fails to restore the original text,** the number is still flagged; it just is not
  rewritten. This happens when the verifier cannot safely tell which player the number belongs to.

**Audit trail.** The injection test found real verifier bugs, all fixed before the held-out run:

- Decimal claims matched integer truths ("1.5" counted as rank 2).†
- Sums and differences of row values were accepted anywhere ("Netherlands – 8" when 8 = 5 + 3).†
- "followed by" counted as comparison wording.†
- "World Cup" blocked attributing a number to the player before it.†

The naive-baseline scorer had two more bugs:

- **Rounding:** rounded stored truths made correct "65.38%"† claims count as wrong, which inflated an early
  run to 41.9%†.
- **Team questions:** these were included at first.

## Training

- **Data:** 3,096 train pairs from 697 specs (3,925 pairs from 880 specs in all,
  split by spec: 697 / 86 / 97).
- **Config:** LoRA r=16, alpha=32, all linear layers; lr 2e-4 cosine; 3
  epochs; batch 16; bf16; max length 1,024; completion-only loss.
- **Run:** 582 steps, 30 min on one H200. Final val loss 0.0019. TensorBoard logs are in
  `models/sft-v1/runs/`; the run record is in `runs/sft-v1/`.
- **Pilot:** 1,112 pairs, 2 epochs, 6.5 min. Val 98.3, dev/hard
  83.3.

GRPO (stretch goal) has not been run. On these sets the SFT student has little headroom left. Decide once the
hand-written set exists.
